lesson.title: Uphill Lines: Recognizing and Computing Positive Slope
lesson.summary: A positive slope means a line climbs from left to right, and it shows up any time the output grows as the input grows.
lesson.body:
Slope tells you both how steep a line is and which direction it leans, and the sign of the slope carries the direction information. When a line has positive slope, it rises as you scan it from left to right: as the x-coordinate increases, the y-coordinate also increases. Picture walking along the line from left to right, if you are walking uphill, the slope is positive.

Positive slope shows up constantly in real situations where more input produces more output. A worker who earns a fixed hourly wage sees total pay increase as hours worked increase. A car that accelerates from a stop covers more distance as time increases. Savings in an account earning simple interest grow larger as more months pass. In every one of these, both quantities move in the same direction together, and that shared direction is the signature of positive slope.

Consider the points (1, 2) and (4, 11), and use the slope formula to find the slope of the line through them. With x1 = 1, y1 = 2, x2 = 4, y2 = 11, the formula gives m = (11 minus 2) divided by (4 minus 1), which is 9 divided by 3, and that simplifies to 3. The slope is 3, and since 3 is greater than 0, the slope is positive. You can see the uphill behavior directly in the coordinates: as x went from 1 to 4, an increase of 3, y went from 2 to 11, an increase of 9. Both changes were increases, so the line climbs.

The size of a positive slope also tells you how steep the climb is, not just that it climbs. A slope of 3 means that for every 1 unit you move to the right, the line rises 3 units, which is fairly steep. A slope of 1/2 would mean the line only climbs half a unit for every unit moved right, a much gentler uphill path. Both are positive, both climb left to right, but 3 is steeper than 1/2 because it is the larger number.

A quick way to sanity-check whether a slope should be positive, before you even finish the formula, is to look at whether both coordinates increased together or both decreased together when moving from one point to the other. If x increased and y also increased, or if x decreased and y also decreased, the slope will be positive, because a negative divided by a negative, like a positive divided by a positive, always gives a positive result. That mental check is a fast way to catch an arithmetic slip after you compute a slope with the formula.

Positive slope also matters once you start writing equations of lines, since the sign of m in slope-intercept form, y equals mx plus b, tells you immediately what the graph looks like before you plot a single point. An equation like y equals 3x minus 1 has slope 3, so you already know its graph climbs left to right without needing to substitute numbers first. When two lines both have positive slope, the one with the larger slope value climbs more steeply. Comparing the earlier line, slope 3, with a second line of slope 1/2, the slope 3 line rises 3 units for every 1 unit moved right, while the slope 1/2 line only rises half a unit in the same horizontal distance, so the slope 3 line reaches any given height in far less horizontal distance and looks noticeably steeper on a graph.
